skills.name: Written preparation: a money-and-amount listening script

note.text: This is written preparation for a listening lesson. Read the original script for meaning, key information and unknown words. It provides no audio and cannot assess listening comprehension. A teacher or recording should later supply an oral version; the questions here assess the written script. Identify the main idea and locate evidence for each answer. A question may concern a detail, reason, sequence or word in context. If the text omits information, do not supply an invented fact. A plausible outcome is not necessarily a reported result.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to extract an amount and transaction sequence from a written script before later listening practice. Builds on: figures, number words and currency labels. Leads to: clear numerical references in talks and reports.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original script: In a fictional school exercise, Bih brings {5000} CFA francs. A notebook costs {1500} CFA francs and a folder costs {1000}. She chooses the notebook and postpones the folder. The model therefore leaves {5000-1500} CFA francs. All amounts are invented. The script gives no real seller or bank details and supplies no exchange rate.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Read the whole passage before answering. Point to a phrase supporting the answer and explain any inference. When summarising, preserve who did what and whether an action was planned or completed. These original classroom texts are not extracts from prescribed literature.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: An explicit detail is always something invented by the reader. Correction: Direct information appears in the passage.

An absent detail must always be replaced with a guessed number. Correction: A faithful answer acknowledges missing information.

pick.q:
Original script: In a fictional school exercise, Bih brings {5000} CFA francs. A notebook costs {1500} CFA francs and a folder costs {1000}. She chooses the notebook and postpones the folder. The model therefore leaves {5000-1500} CFA francs. All amounts are invented. The script gives no real seller or bank details and supplies no exchange rate.
What does Bih buy in the script?
w: A phone not mentioned in the script.
e: The folder is postponed.
She chooses the notebook.
No phone purchase is described.
pick.y: The script explicitly names the chosen item.

pick.q:
Original script: In a fictional school exercise, Bih brings {5000} CFA francs. A notebook costs {1500} CFA francs and a folder costs {1000}. She chooses the notebook and postpones the folder. The model therefore leaves {5000-1500} CFA francs. All amounts are invented. The script gives no real seller or bank details and supplies no exchange rate.
What amount remains in the model?
e: That incorrectly subtracts the postponed folder.
Spending reduces, rather than increases, the balance.
That is the notebook price, not the remainder.
pick.y: Subtract only the chosen notebook from the starting amount.

pick.q:
Original script: In a fictional school exercise, Bih brings {5000} CFA francs. A notebook costs {1500} CFA francs and a folder costs {1000}. She chooses the notebook and postpones the folder. The model therefore leaves {5000-1500} CFA francs. All amounts are invented. The script gives no real seller or bank details and supplies no exchange rate.

pick.r: It is not bought in the stated transaction.
w: Its price is definitely paid already.
It is the same object as the notebook.
e: Postponing gives no free-price claim.
The script excludes the purchase now.
The script names different items.
pick.y: Preserve the difference between the current choice and the delayed one.

pick.q: Check this reading claim about the original passage: A missing price or name can be guessed and reported as stated fact.
pick.r: No: report only what the passage supplies or supports.
w: Yes: every guess is an explicit detail.
Yes: a familiar name must be the writer’s chosen name.
Yes: a price from another story must apply.
e: A guess is not direct information.
Familiarity does not provide textual evidence.
A different story supplies no fact about this passage.

pick.q: Check this reading claim about the original passage: A summary should preserve the central actions rather than add an unrelated event.
pick.r: Yes: keep the summary faithful to the passage.
w: No: summaries must invent a new ending.
No: any unrelated opinion replaces the main idea.
No: a summary must be longer than every source text.
e: A summary does not invent a resolution.
An unrelated opinion is not a faithful summary.
Length alone is not the criterion.
pick.y: Select and connect the important points without invention.

pick.q: Check this reading claim about the original passage: A proposed action proves that the action has already been completed.
pick.r: No: a proposal and a completed event are different.
w: Yes: every suggestion is a reported result.
Yes: future wording is always past evidence.
Yes: planning proves every intended outcome.
e: A suggestion is not a result.
Tense and meaning matter.
A plan can fail or change.
pick.y: Preserve the status and time of the action.

pick.q: Check this reading claim about the original passage: An inference should be linked to a clue, rather than just an interesting possibility.
pick.r: Yes: explain which textual detail supports it.
w: No: all possible events are proven.
No: a confident voice establishes every claim.
e: Evidence matters to the inference.
Possible is not the same as established.
Confidence does not replace textual support.
